newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan frets as legislator lands on disputed isles.
newsitem.headline: Japan frets as legislator lands on disputed isles.

text.p: A Japanese legislator and three people accompanying him on Tuesday visited one of a group of islands in the East China Sea disputed by Japan, China and Taiwan in a gesture the Tokyo government swiftly repudiated.

The group headed by Shingo Nishimura, a conservative member of the main opposition New Frontier Party (Shinshinto), inspected the security situation and held a brief commemorative ceremony on the Senkaku Islands, known in Chinese as the Diaoyu Islands, Nishimura's office said in a statement.
Japan's coastguard, the Maritime Safety Agency, confirmed that the group landed at 8.30 a.m. (2330 GMT Monday) on the largest of the islands, which lie 1,600 km (1,000 miles) southwest of Tokyo.
"We believe this landing on the Senkaku Islands will be the starting point for an awakening of national consciousness and the rebirth of a Japan with pride," the statement said.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, however, was quick to distance the central government from Nishimura's group, which included former cabinet minister Shintaro Ishihara, author of the 1980s nationalist treatise "A Japan That Can Say No".

"It is well-known that the owner of the land has refused to allow landings there. Do members of parliament have the right to completely ignore that?" a clearly displeased Hashimoto told reporters in parliament.

The Hashimoto government's spokesman, Seiroku Kajiyama, told a news conference that while the islands were Japanese territory, the group's actions were "extremely regrettable" and should not be allowed to damage Japan-China relations.

The rocky cluster of uninhabited islands has ignited fiery nationalist passions in Chinese communities in Hong Kong and Taiwan since a Japanese right-wing group built a makeshift lighthouse there last July.
The lighthouse drew a flotilla of vessels in the months that followed carrying Taiwanese and Hong Kong Chinese protestors, several of whom briefly landed on the Japanese-administered islands.
Last September, a Hong Kong activist drowned when he jumped into stormy waters near the islands to press China's claim.
In February, Japan sent a letter to U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan in which it sought to have Tokyo's position on the islands included in a U.N. report on the law of the sea.

"In view of the history of the Senkaku Islands and in the light of the relevant principles of international law, there is no question that the islands are an integral part of the territory of Japan, and that Japan has always exercised effective control over them. It is thus the position of the government of Japan that no question of territorial title should arise with respect to those islands," the letter said.
China says its ownership of the islands dates back to ancient times.

In Tuesday's landing, Ishihara remained in the boat and did not actually set foot on the island. The group criticised the central government in Tokyo for labelling a landing on the Senkakus last month by local assembly members from Okinawa, which administers the disputed islands, "a provocative act".
The statement said: "The Senkaku Islands are indisputably Japan's territory. It is a matter of course that a member of parliament should survey Japanese territory."
